messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mr. Pham had lived a relatively quiet life until his marriage to Ms. Nguyen took an unexpected turn six months ago. The abuse he endured was not only physically brutal but psychologically devastating. One particularly violent incident stands out in Mr. Pham's fragmented memories: the day when Ms. Nguyen, in a fit of rage, attacked him with a broken vase from their living room. The sharp edges left deep gashes on his arms and face, leaving indelible marks both physical and psychological. Since that fateful day, feeling tired or uncomfortable has become unbearably triggering for Mr. Pham. These triggers often plunge him into a state of hypervigilance, where he constantly feels unsafe unless his back is against a wall in any room he enters. This heightened sense of danger makes him frequently check behind him to ensure no one is following him. On more than one occasion at work as a tax inspector, Mr. Pham has found himself leaving meetings abruptly when sudden memories of the attack flood his mind, causing intense discomfort and panic. These fragmented and uncontrolled memories often surface unexpectedly during routine tasks at home or office. For instance, while sorting through documents in his office, the sight of a broken pen can send him into a flashback where he relives the moment Ms. Nguyen shattered the vase against him. This intrusion of memory fragments reinforces his negative appraisals: Mr. Pham has come to believe that nothing good will happen to him anymore and that he feels dehumanized, more like an object than a person. His fear of unpredictability further exacerbates these symptoms. When attending social gatherings or even family events, the unpredictability of interactions triggers intense feelings of threat and anxiety. Mr. Pham’s negative appraisals intensify as he begins to believe that betrayal is inevitable, given his past experience with someone he trusted deeply. This belief often leads him into a cycle where he becomes increasingly vigilant and suspicious in all situations, which further reinforces his sense of danger. At work, these triggers manifest through frequent absences or sudden departures from meetings due to overwhelming flashbacks and anxiety attacks. His colleagues have noticed the changes but are unaware of their root cause. Mr. Pham’s relationships with his coworkers have become strained as he withdraws socially and struggles to maintain focus on his tasks. Mr. Pham's deteriorating mental state has also affected his personal life significantly. He has become more isolated from friends and family, spending long hours at home trying to avoid unpredictable situations that could trigger memories or feelings of threat. Even simple activities like grocery shopping can be overwhelming due to the unpredictability of crowds and environments. The weight of these experiences has left Mr. Pham feeling utterly defeated. He is acutely aware that his negative appraisals have become self-fulfilling prophecies, leading him into a cycle where he feels constantly threatened and dehumanized. The unpredictability of daily life only serves to reinforce these feelings, making it nearly impossible for him to find moments of peace or security. It was the realization that his quality of life has severely deteriorated that finally brought Mr. Pham to seek help. He is most afraid of being trapped in this state indefinitely but also hopes to regain a sense of control and dignity. Through therapy, he seeks to understand how these triggers and negative appraisals interact, and how he can break free from the cycle of fear and dehumanization that has come to define his life. Mr. Pham’s journey towards healing is fraught with challenges, but he remains determined to reclaim a sense of normalcy and self-worth.
